The Battle of Manzikert. On the twenty-sixth of August, ten seventy-one, near the fortress city of Manzikert in Armenian territory, the Seljuk Sultan Alp Arslan decisively defeated Byzantine Emperor Romanus IV Diogenes. The Byzantine army numbered thirty to forty thousand troops, while the Seljuk force was roughly half that size—fifteen thousand. Yet the Seljuks won a catastrophic victory.

Romanus IV Diogenes led the Byzantine forces directly into an ambush. The Seljuks feigned retreat, drawing the Byzantine army into exposed terrain. Then they surrounded the Byzantine forces completely and broke them utterly. Romanus IV was captured and ransomed, and he returned to Constantinople in shame. His defeat severely damaged imperial prestige and weakened his position at court.

The military loss was only the beginning of the catastrophe. Anatolia—historically the heart of the Byzantine Empire and the source of its soldiers and resources—was now lost to Seljuk control. This loss shifted the entire balance of power in the eastern Mediterranean. The Byzantine Empire, once the dominant power of the region, was reduced to a shrinking coastal state. In desperation, the Byzantine emperors sent requests for military aid to the Pope in the West. These requests were a key factor in prompting the First Crusade from ten ninety-six onward. Manzikert marked the beginning of Turkish-Muslim dominance in Anatolia and the permanent weakening of the ancient Byzantine Empire. One battle on an Armenian plain set off a cascade of consequences that would reshape the medieval world.
